props.title: Mr. Death

sections.content: Mr. Death: The Rise and Fall of Fred A. Leuchter, Jr. (1999) stands as one of Errol Morris's most unsettling documentaries, using his signature Interrotron interview style to probe the mind of Fred Leuchter, an execution equipment designer who became an infamous Holocaust denier. The film builds like a psychological thriller, starting with Leuchter's bizarre career "improving" electric chairs and lethal injection systems before his catastrophic involvement with Holocaust denial. Morris's approach in this film influenced later works like The Fog of War (2003) and The Unknown Known (2013), showing how seemingly rational people can descend into dangerous delusions.

sections.content: The film's examination of self-deception connects to other documentaries about people blinded by their own expertise or certainty. A Brief History of Time (1991) shows Stephen Hawking's brilliant yet humble approach to cosmic mysteries, while Into the Abyss (2011) explores capital punishment through Werner Herzog's probing conversations with death row inmates and officers. Morris's technique of letting subjects reveal themselves through extended interviews influenced countless later documentaries.

The technical aspects of Mr. Death showcase Morris's innovative visual style. He combines Leuchter's direct-to-camera interviews with stylized reenactments and archival footage, creating a disturbing portrait of how "professional" methodology can be used to support horrific conclusions. This approach influenced later films like The Imposter (2012) and Tower (2016) in their use of mixed media to explore dark subject matter. SUBHEAD: The Ethics of Documentary Representation

sections.content: Morris's handling of Leuchter raises crucial questions about documentary ethics and the filmmaker's responsibility when presenting controversial subjects. Unlike the more confrontational approach of films like Shoah (1985) or The Last Days (1998), Morris allows Leuchter's self-incrimination to unfold naturally, trusting viewers to recognize the horror of his conclusions. This technique influenced later documentaries like Going Clear (2015) and The World According to Dick Cheney (2013).
